::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
set.seed(3)
```
:::




**The question.** In SIR, every infected person can infect every susceptible person (mass action). What happens when people can only infect their neighbours?

## A cellular automaton

Each cell of an $L \times L$ grid is one individual: susceptible (0), infected (1) or recovered (2). In every time step:

- a susceptible cell with $k$ infected neighbours (up, down, left, right) becomes infected with probability $1 - (1 - p)^k$;
- an infected cell recovers with probability $q$.

This is an *individual-based* model: no compartment proportions and no ODEs, just rules for each individual. Counting neighbours with shifted copies of the grid is fast, even in R.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shift <- function(m, dr, dc) {                 # shift a matrix, filling with 0
  L <- nrow(m); out <- matrix(0, L, L)
  rs <- max(1, 1 + dr):min(L, L + dr); cs <- max(1, 1 + dc):min(L, L + dc)
  out[rs, cs] <- m[rs - dr, cs - dc]
  out
}

ca_sir <- function(L = 101, p = 0.3, q = 0.2, steps = 150, mixed = FALSE) {
  grid <- matrix(0L, L, L)
  grid[ceiling(L / 2), ceiling(L / 2)] <- 1L   # one infected cell in the middle
  snaps <- list(); cum <- numeric(steps)
  for (t in 1:steps) {
    inf <- (grid == 1) * 1
    k <- if (mixed) {
      4 * mean(inf)                            # well-mixed: 4 contacts drawn from everyone
    } else {
      shift(inf, 1, 0) + shift(inf, -1, 0) + shift(inf, 0, 1) + shift(inf, 0, -1)
    }
    new_inf <- grid == 0 & runif(L^2) < 1 - (1 - p)^k
    recover <- grid == 1 & runif(L^2) < q
    grid[new_inf] <- 1L
    grid[recover] <- 2L
    cum[t] <- sum(grid > 0)
    if (t %in% c(20, 50, 80)) snaps[[as.character(t)]] <- grid
  }
  list(snaps = snaps, cum = cum)
}

local_run <- ca_sir()
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
snap_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(local_run$snaps), function(t) {
  g <- local_run$snaps[[t]]
  data.frame(x = rep(1:ncol(g), each = nrow(g)), y = rep(1:nrow(g), ncol(g)),
             state = factor(c(g), levels = 0:2, labels = c("S", "I", "R")),
             time = paste("t =", t))
}))
snap_df$time <- factor(snap_df$time, levels = paste("t =", names(local_run$snaps)))
ggplot(snap_df, aes(x, y, fill = state)) +
  geom_raster() + facet_wrap(~time) + coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(S = "grey92", I = "#E69F00", R = "#56B4E9")) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) + labs(fill = NULL)
```

![The epidemic spreads as a ring: infected cells (orange) form a travelling front, with recovered cells (blue) behind it.](05-spatial_files/figure-html/fig-snapshots-1.png){#fig-snapshots width=672}
:::

## Waves grow slowly

With mass action, cases grow exponentially at first. On a grid, new infections can only happen at the *front* of the epidemic. The front moves at a roughly constant speed, so the infected area grows like $t^2$.

To compare like with like, we run the same model with the 4 contacts drawn from the whole population instead of the neighbours (`mixed = TRUE`). This has the same $p$, the same $q$ and the same number of contacts.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mixed_run <- ca_sir(mixed = TRUE)
growth <- rbind(data.frame(time = 1:150, cum = local_run$cum, contacts = "local (grid)"),
                data.frame(time = 1:150, cum = mixed_run$cum, contacts = "well mixed"))
ggplot(growth, aes(time, cum, colour = contacts)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`local (grid)` = "#E69F00", `well mixed` = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Time step", y = "Cumulative infections (log)", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cumulative infections: well-mixed contacts (grey) grow exponentially; local contacts (orange) grow like t². Log scale.](05-spatial_files/figure-html/fig-growth-1.png){#fig-growth width=672}
:::
:::




(The well-mixed run can die out by chance in its first steps. If it does, change the seed, and remember [T2](02-chance.qmd).)

## Exercises

1. Lower $p$ step by step. Below some value the infection no longer spreads across the grid, even though each infected cell still infects more than one neighbour on average in a fully susceptible neighbourhood. Why? (Keyword: *percolation*.)
2. Fit $\log(\text{cum})$ against $\log(t)$ for the local run. Is the slope close to 2?
3. Vaccinate a random 30% of cells before the start (set them to 2). Compare with the well-mixed version at the same coverage.
